analysis.one_liner: Requires mediation and, if needed, binding arbitration so employers and newly certified unions must reach a first contract.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up by the House committee it was sent to, drew no cosponsors, and died at the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, when workers vote to form a union, the employer and the union must bargain in good faith toward a first contract — but there is no deadline, and some employers simply stall until workers give up. This bill would change that: if no first contract is reached within 60 days of the union being certified, the two sides would have to use a mediator; if mediation failed within another 30 days, either side could send the unresolved issues to binding arbitration, where an impartial arbitrator decides the terms. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at newly organized workplaces. When employees vote for a union, the contract that follows sets their wages, benefits, and working conditions; without a contract, a union win can mean very little. This bill would put a clock on that bargaining — 60 days to a mediator, then binding arbitration — so an employer could not simply stall until the campaign's momentum fades. Workers who organized in good faith would be far more likely to actually get the terms they voted for.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Newly unionized workers awaiting a first contract

how_it_helps.text: If a newly certified union and its employer cannot agree on a first contract within 60 days, the bill requires mediation of the disputed issues.

If mediation does not produce an agreement within 30 days after a mediator is chosen, either side can send the remaining disputes to binding arbitration — meaning an impartial arbitrator, not either party, would decide the terms.
Mediators could be chosen jointly by the parties, or by the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service if they cannot agree, so a single employer could not stall the process by refusing to pick one.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially those who currently benefit from slow-walking first contract negotiations. Binding arbitration means a third party could set contract terms — including pay and benefits — that the employer did not agree to. Business groups generally oppose mandatory first-contract arbitration for this reason, though no such opposition appears in this bill's record.

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration means a third-party arbitrator, not the employer or the union, would have final say over wages, benefits, and other first-contract terms if mediation failed — terms neither side actually agreed to.

The deadlines are tight: mediation would have to begin within 60 days of a union election and arbitration could follow within 30 days after a mediator is chosen, which employers could argue is too little time for genuinely complex first contracts.
The bill attracted no cosponsors and no committee action beyond referral, so there is no record of any hearing or debate on these concerns in this Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but narrower than it might sound: the bill would not create a single union job or raise a wage by itself; it would only speed up the first contract after workers win an election, which is a known bottleneck where campaigns often stall out. Mediation is a low-cost step. Binding arbitration is a stronger intervention, and the good-faith objection is that it hands a third party power to set wages and workplace rules that both sides did not agree to, which employers argue raises risk and could discourage hiring. Supporters respond that the deadline pressure of possible arbitration is precisely what pushes both sides to settle on their own, and that it restores the promise workers relied on when they voted for a union. On balance, an honest weighing favors the bill for workers who organize, while acknowledging that the time limits are tight and that arbitration outcomes can disappoint both sides.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee, was passed down to a subcommittee in April 2013, and was never scheduled for a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 4, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On April 23, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it remained.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action was taken before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill did not carry over.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who prefer to bargain without a binding deadline keep the current system, where a first contract can be delayed indefinitely after workers vote for a union. Workers who organize gain nothing from this Congress.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after it was referred on January 4, 2013.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat introduced the bill and not one member of either party cosponsored it; the Republican-controlled committee took no action, so the bill died on party-lined lines without a single recorded vote.

industries.industry: Employers facing new union organizing (retail, services, manufacturing)
industries.note: Employers would no longer be able to slow-walk or refuse first contracts indefinitely after losing a union election; binding arbitration could impose terms on them. From the worker's side, this targets the well-documented gap between winning an election and actually getting a contract.

Newly certified unions would get a path to a binding first contract instead of open-ended bargaining, strengthening the value of organizing. This runs alongside workers' interests, since a contract is what turns a union vote into real wages and rules.

industries.industry: Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and arbitrators
industries.note: The bill routes all stalled first-contract disputes through the federal mediation service and private arbitrators, creating a steady stream of cases. This is the mechanism the bill relies on, not a lobbying interest identified in the record.
